title: Mastering Go Concurrency: Goroutines, Channels, and Select Patterns
description: A comprehensive hands-on course on building highly concurrent, lock-free, scalable backend systems in Go using worker pools, fan-out/fan-in pipelines, context cancellation, and race detection.
body: Master Communicating Sequential Processes (CSP) in Go. This course covers everything from goroutine scheduler mechanics to production worker pools, rate limiters, context timeouts, and data race elimination.

sections.title: Section 1: Concurrency Primitives & Go Scheduler Internal Architecture

lessons.title: Lesson 1.1: OS Threads vs. Go Scheduler M:N Model
lessons.body:
### The Scenario: Thread Starvation Crisis
Imagine running a backend service handling 50,000 concurrent HTTP requests. On traditional systems allocating 1MB OS thread stacks, 50,000 threads consume 50GB of RAM just for stack overhead, causing kernel thrashing and OS crash.

### Go's M:N Runtime Scheduler Solution
Go multiplexes N goroutines onto M operating system threads using P logical processors:
- **G (Goroutine):** Starts with an initial lightweight ~2KB resizable stack.
- **M (Machine):** OS kernel thread.
- **P (Processor):** Context resource managing runnable Goroutine queues (`GOMAXPROCS`).

```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"runtime"
	"sync"
)

func main() {
	fmt.Printf("Logical CPUs (P): %d\n", runtime.NumCPU())
	var wg sync.WaitGroup
	for i := 0; i < 5; i++ {
		wg.Add(1)
		go func(id int) {
			defer wg.Done()
			fmt.Printf("Goroutine %d executing\n", id)
		}(i)
	}
	wg.Wait()
}
```

lessons.title: Lesson 1.2: Channel Internals: Unbuffered vs. Buffered Channels
lessons.body:
### Unbuffered vs. Buffered Synchronization
- **Unbuffered Channels (`make(chan T)`):** Guarantee strict synchronization. Producer blocks until consumer is ready to receive.
- **Buffered Channels (`make(chan T, N)`):** Decouple producer and consumer execution up to buffer capacity N.

```go
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	ch := make(chan string, 2)
	ch <- "payload-1"
	ch <- "payload-2"
	
	fmt.Println(<-ch)
	fmt.Println(<-ch)
}
```

Lesson 2.2: Fan-Out, Fan-In Pipeline Stream Processing
lessons.body:
### Fan-Out & Fan-In Architecture
- **Fan-Out:** Multiple workers read from a single input stream channel to process tasks in parallel.
- **Fan-In:** A single aggregator function combines multiple output channels into one unified result stream.

lessons.title: Lesson 3.1: Eliminating Data Races with Race Detector (`go test -race`)
lessons.body:
### The Silent Corruption Bug
Concurrent writes to non-atomic shared variables without mutex locking cause silent data corruption in multi-core processors. Always execute `go test -race ./...` in CI pipelines.
